title: Multiple Chronic COnditions: MultiPle dAta SouRcEs (MC COMPARE)
text:
High blood pressure can lead to heart attacks, strokes, and kidney failure, amongst other outcomes, but
lowering blood pressure too much leads to bad outcomes. This study will help understand how more
information about certain people, especially those with multiple chronic conditions and older adults, can help
balance the risks and benefits.

title: The role of mobile elements in chromatin regulation
text:
Transposable element insertions and short-tandem-repeat expansions are widespread sources of structural
variation that can remodel chromatin architecture and perturb gene expression across the human genome.
Their dysregulation is increasingly implicated in neurodegenerative and neuromuscular disorders, cancers, and
age-related decline, underscoring an urgent need to define how these hidden variants influence disease risk.
This project will apply advanced long-read sequencing, CRISPR-based enrichment, and integrative
computational modeling to identify and mechanistically characterize these variants at population and single-cell
resolution, generating insights that will inform precision diagnostics and interventions and thereby promote
public health.

title: The Platelet Transcriptome and Organ Failure After Injury: Discovering Molecular Biomarkers and Preventative Targets through Interrogating Novel RNA Modifications
text:
The proposed research is relevant globally to public health because each year injury is a leading cause of over
four million deaths, and over half of survivors suffer from organ failure. Platelets contribute to the pathobiology
of organ failure through thromboinflammation, and in many diseases characterized by organ failure, studying
the platelet transcriptome has improved mechanistic understandings and driven exploration of platelet-based
therapeutics. Platelets are anucleate and lack RNA synthesis, providing the cleanest transcriptomic view of
RNA modification in human biology; thus, this proposal seeks to re-imagine how we understand, measure, and
intervene on early alterations in platelets after injury by focusing on the platelet transcriptome to 1) identify
novel molecular biomarkers and preventative targets of development of organ failure after injury, and 2)
innovate our understanding of physiologically driven RNA modification through the ideal anucleate biology of
platelets under the optimal acute physiologic changes of injury.

title: Core D: Cancer Models
text:
The Cancer Models Core (Core D) will facilitate the translation of novel therapies into the clinic by providing
SPORE investigators with ovarian cancer patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models in immunocompromised mice,
a syngeneic model in immunocompetent mice, and ex vivo 3D cultures of primary and PDX tumors. PDX tumors
were collected at surgery from patients with ovarian, fallopian tube, and primary peritoneal cancer made available
through this Core for current and future use in research projects designed to improve the treatment of ovarian
cancer. The Cancer Models Core collaborates directly with Core B for tumor acquisition and with Core C for
genomic and clinical data correlation.

title: A molecular pathway that links N-glycosylation to birth defects
text:
A molecular pathway that links N-glycosylation to birth defects
Damage to cell-cell communications systems can cause a variety of human birth defects. We have uncovered
a system that tunes the volume of a key developmental signal between cells. By understanding how this
amplifier works, we hope to lay the foundation for new diagnostic, preventative and therapeutic strategies to
ameliorate the burden of birth defect syndromes.

title: Defining and Controlling Protein-RNA interactions in editing pathways
text:
RNA editing catalyzed by the ADAR enzymes is perturbed in a variety of human
diseases and oligonucleotide recruitment of ADARs to carry out therapeutic edits is a
promising new strategy. The proposed studies will extend our basic understanding of
the process of RNA editing, lead to new methods for the control of RNA editing and
advance approaches for the modification and optimization of therapeutic RNAs.

title: FlexLock - A novel anchoring guide catheter to simplify transradial complex percutaneous coronary interventions
text:
Adequate backup force and catheter stability during transradial complex PCI are necessary to treat
coronary artery disease. Current devices often sacrifice lumen space to achieve stability, leading to poor
procedural outcomes, increased procedure time, and risk of complications. Nimble Surgical’s FlexLock
catheter with concurrent active and passive support provides higher backup force and perfusion in a
smaller profile, increasing device delivery efficiency and simplifying heart procedures.

title: Development of a human intestinal microphysiological system for the study of immune responses to protozoan parasites
text:
Parasites infect millions of people every year, but there are no effective vaccines against food or waterborne
parasite. We will generate 3D gut-vasculature lumen models, where parasites are introduced into the intestinal
epithelium and human immune cells into the vasculature to monitor immune response and parasitic disease.
For this proposal, we will use the orally infectious stages of the protozoan parasites Toxoplasma gondii and
Entamoeba histolytica, and determine that human immune response that controls these infections.

title: Cerebral organoid and IPSC derived microglia: Modeling of HIV and methamphetamine co-morbidity
text:
Despite the success of cART, high prevalence of HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) poses a
major challenge for the society. This proposal focuses on the use of a novel 3-dimensional organoid co-culture
model to decipher mechanistic pathways that underlie abnormalities in neuronal connectivity as seen in HAND.

title: THE INTEGRATED STRESS RESPONSE IN GBM PATHOGENESIS AND RESPONSE TO THERAPY
text:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive, incurable type of brain tumor endowed with an ability to
adapt and survive under high-stress conditions. We identified molecular targets capable of
modulating stress signaling to support tumor growth and confer therapeutic resistance in GBM.
Our proposed studies will determine whether modulating these targets could impair tumor growth
and increase the efficacy of targeted therapeutics currently used in the clinic to treat brain tumors.

title: Circuit pathophysiology, phenotypic heterogeneity and translational electrophysiological biomarkers in mouse models of FXS
text: Project 2: Circuit pathophysiology, phenotypic heterogeneity and translational electrophysiological biomarkers in mouse models of FXS. Translational biomarkers for Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) were suggested from the findings of our research team that sensory circuits are hyperexcitable in both FXS patients and Fmr1 KO mice, as measured with electroencephalogram (EEG) in mice and humans and in in vitro brain slices. Based on this idea, our team of investigators, working closely together within an NIH Collaborative Center for Fragile X Research, has discovered multiple neurophysiological signatures of FXS, both in the resting state and with sensory, or sound-evoked EEG, that are remarkably conserved between FXS patients and Fmr1 KO mice. Our progress in translational neurophysiology research has benefited greatly from our development of multi- electrode array (MEA) EEG for awake, behaving mice that provides direct parallel to high-density EEG studies in FXS patients. In particular, we discovered EEG biomarkers of enhanced resting state gamma power and impaired auditory chirp-induced cortical synchronization in both Fmr1 KO mice and FXS patients. In the current group of studies, we propose to: (1) define circuit pathophysiology of FXS and develop translational EEG biomarkers; (2) define phenotypic heterogeneity in electrophysiology in female Fmr1 KO and heterozygous mice; and (3) determine effects of target modulation on EEG in Fmr1 KO mice. Both (1) and (3) will be done in coordination with clinicians in Project 1 to evaluate analogous EEG biomarkers across species and test identical drugs. Both (2) and (3) will be done in coordination with Project 3 researchers working on in vitro slice preparations to identify synaptic and cellular deficits. Thus, Project 2 will be a critical hub of the center by translating cellular and molecular level analyses to clinical approaches using network and layer-specific MEA EEG analysis. We anticipate identification of novel biomarker-based drug targets for treatment of FXS. Our approach will serve as a paradigm for drug discovery in neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: "Project 2" Microprocessor overload in gamma-herpesviral oncogenesis
text:
The Epstein Barr virus (EBV) is a primary causative agent in HIV-associated lymphomas. Based on preliminary
studies in tissue culture and clinical models, we hypothesize that two large EBV miRNA clusters are critical
players in eliciting the tumor phenotype through altering the immune cell microenvironment via their canonical
functions and cell growth and/or protection against cell death through a previously unknown non-canonical
mechanism.

title: Dissecting circadian chronoarchitecture of the intestine
text:
Misalignment between the body clock and environmental cues, as occurs in shift workers, has been linked to a
variety of intestinal disorders, including irritable bowel syndrome. This proposal aims to elucidate how intestinal
clocks are organized in response to dynamic changes in light and food availability and how their disruption
contributes to disease, using a novel approach to measure circadian rhythms in individual intestinal cells. Insights
from these studies could inform strategies to prevent functional defects caused by circadian misalignment and
guide the development of time-tailored therapies.

title: Gene Delivery
text:
Narrative Gene Delivery Core
The Gene Delivery Core will serve the UC Berkeley Vision Science community by designing
and producing viral vectors, introducing new gene delivery technologies to users, and assisting
researchers in generating transgenic animal models.

title: Preclinical and Clincial Outcomes
text: The primary goal of the Preclinical & Clinical Outcomes (PCO) Core is to provide the infrastructure, expertise and resources to support bi-directional translational efforts spanning animal and human research. Combining the expertise of neurobehavioral tools in animal models and neuropsychiatric assessment methods in humans will ensure the use and development of maximally relevant tasks and measures, helping to address challenges in translational research in IDD. The PCO Core will provide investigators with a battery of validated assays for rodents and humans, with a focus on creating a translational pipeline, as well as harmonizing measures across studies. In addition, the PCO Core will provide access and training on the use of additional behavioral assays that will allow IDDRC investigators to perform critical secondary or follow-up studies to better understand the nature of any behavioral abnormality detected with a primary behavioral test battery. The Animal Phenotyping & Preclinical Endpoints sub-core provides resources for investigators to perform behavioral assessment across various domains in rodent models. This core also focuses on development of robust preclinical outcome measures for assessment of potential interventions, serving as surrogate endpoints in treatment paradigms for potential therapies. The animal phenotyping sub-core provides high quality, cost effective behavioral assessments in rodent models, expert consultation for experimental design and data analysis and training investigators to conduct behavior assessments independently. It also offers educational workshops on various topics and data analysis, technical issues, trouble-shooting and development of novel assays as preclinical outcome measures. The Human Phenotyping and Neuropsych Measures sub-core provides neurobehavioral and neuropsychiatric assessment tools, comprising questionnaire-based methods, structured clinical interviews, and task-based measures. Some of the innovative approaches provided by the human phenotyping sub-core includes a novel computer vision-based technique for quantifying dynamics of facial expression, posture, and gaze ("automated multimodal analysis"), and bio-behavioral sensing, to move beyond traditional assessment approaches. Investigators can access consultation and guidance regarding developing phenotyping batteries, which may involve the creation or utilization of novel approaches. They can also access training and/or supervision in implementing and analyzing varied tasks, together with quality assurance resources. The human phenotyping sub-core will also provide direct service in implementing tailored phenotyping approaches for mental health conditions frequently prevalent in IDD. Finally, investigators can access consultation regarding building animal to human models of disease state to facilitate translation. Thus, the PCO Core's set of unique resources and broad expertise provides IDDRC Investigators a cost- effective and flexible means for conducting cross-species translational research in IDD. .

title: Targeting RNA G-Quadruplex Structures to Restore TDP-43 Cryptic Exon Repression in ALS/FTD
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are fatal brain disorders in which
mislocalization of the protein TDP-43 causes harmful errors in RNA processing that kill neurons. In this project,
we will map and validate specialized RNA structures called G-quadruplexes that guide TDP-43 to its proper
targets and then use cutting-edge biochemical assays and machine learning to discover small molecules that
stabilize these structures and restore normal RNA splicing in patient-derived neurons. By correcting the potential
root cause of RNA misprocessing, our work aims to launch a novel class of therapies to protect neurons and
slow disease progression in ALS and FTD.

title: Predicting Recurrent Acute Mental Health Episodes Requiring Emergency Department Visits and/or Hospitalizations Among Midlife Women
text: Midlife women experience biopsychosocial and contextual factors that may increase their risk of recurrent acute mental health episodes requiring emergency department visits and/or hospitalizations. This study will use real-world clinical data and rigorous machine-learning methods to identify measurable factors associated with recurrence, predict risk of recurrent acute mental health episodes, and identify clinically relevant factors contributing to predicted risk. Findings will inform future development of clinical decision support and targeted interventions to prevent recurrent acute mental health episodes and improve mental health outcomes among midlife women.

title: Mechanisms of Cu-binding factors to promote myogenic gene expression
text:
Copper (Cu) is an essential nutrient for healthy muscle development, yet its role in regulating gene
activity and muscle repair remains poorly understood. This project investigates how Cu-binding
proteins control muscle development, regeneration and function, and how Cu imbalance contributes
to disease in Menkes and Wilson disorders. By uncovering these mechanisms, our work aims to fill a
fundamental gap in muscle biology and pave the way for new treatments for both rare genetic
diseases and common muscle-related conditions such as aging and metabolic disorders.

title: Improving surgical outcomes through optimized hernia prediction
text:
Incisional hernia (IH) persists as an unsolved major surgical health problem with a significant
prevalence, insufficient treatments, broad stakeholder impact, diverse risk factors, and challenging
epidemiology. Our proposal addresses barriers to IH prevention through multi-source clinical data designed to
elucidate and discover key mechanistic drivers of hernia and enable development of performance-optimized,
user-informed, parsimonious, specialty-specific models for use within a clinical decision support mobile user
interface (CDS-MUI) that will be tested to identify strategies for widespread implementation. This work will lead
to a broad, significant, and sustained impact on the field, catalyzing a major pivot towards hernia prevention
and enabling precise risk prediction for surgery patients.

title: HIV-1 Env gp160 maturation in the Golgi apparatus
text:
This is highly significant project for the public health because it will elucidate a broad antiviral mechanism,
which will be likely translated into a novel antiviral countermeasure for HIV-1 and other highly pathogenic
human viruses including SARS-CoV2, Ebola viruses, and influenza viruses.
